body: A Kaiser window is a parameterized family of window functions defined by the zeroth-order modified Bessel function. Its formula is: w(n) = I₀(πβ√(1−((2n−(N−1))/(N))²)) / I₀(πβ) for 0 ≤ n ≤ N−1, where I₀ is the zeroth-order modified Bessel function of the first kind, N is the window length, and β is the shape parameter. The β parameter controls the tradeoff between main-lobe width and side-lobe attenuation: β = 0 yields a rectangular window; β = 2.43 is optimal for DFT analysis; β = 3.44 approximates a Hamming window; β = 5 gives ≈−43 dB side lobes; β = 6 gives ≈−47 dB; β ≥ 9 approaches the Blackman-Harris form. The family is designed to achieve the maximum main-lobe concentration for a given side-lobe level — optimal for a specified side-lobe constraint. Persistence mechanism: the Bessel-function formula codified in DSP literature and implemented in all major signal-processing toolkits. [formal: fenestra kaißer | substrate: mind | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.5]

Text-linguistics is a human-made discipline of linguistics — the study of the structure, coherence, and function of extended texts (discourses) as structured wholes that extend beyond the sentence level. Two parameters carve the construct: (1) the unit of analysis is the text or discourse as an integrated semantic-pragmatic entity, governed by relations of cohesion (grammatical and lexical ties across clauses), coherence (understandable logical and semantic connections), and communicative purpose (the function the text serves in interaction); (2) the analytical tools include discourse structure analysis (narrative, argumentative, expository patterns), information structure (theme-rheme, given-new), referential continuity (pronoun chains, anaphora resolution), and textual genre conventions that organize texts for specific communicative situations. Text-linguistics persists as a discipline that produces descriptions of textual organization across languages, models of discourse interpretation, and applications in text technology, rhetoric, discourse analysis, and language pedagogy. Paradigmatic cases: Halliday and Hasan's cohesion analysis, van Dijk's discourse semantics, rhetorical structure theory. [formal: textus-linguistica | substrate: mind | horizon: decades | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.02]

The vocal-tract model is a human-made model of the vocal tract as an acoustic filter cavity in speech production, describing how the shape of the vocal tract resonates to shape the glottal source into speech sounds. Parameters: area function along tract length, formant frequencies and bandwidths, articulatory positions. Persistence mechanism: the model is formalized as acoustic tube theory, implemented in speech synthesis and analysis software, and taught in phonetics; it persists as a reusable filter component of the source-filter framework. [formal: vocal-tract | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.07]

An analytic signal is a human-made complex-valued signal representation constructed from a real-valued signal x(t) by adding its Hilbert transform H{x(t)} as the imaginary component: z(t) = x(t) + j·H{x(t)}. This construction eliminates all negative-frequency components, resulting in a one-sided spectrum. The analytic signal carries three directly accessible parameters: (1) instantaneous amplitude (envelope) A(t) = |z(t)| = √(x(t)² + H{x(t)}²), (2) instantaneous phase φ(t) = arg(z(t)), and (3) instantaneous frequency f_inst(t) = (1/2π)·dφ/dt. These parameters are computable in real time from a single observation, without ensemble averaging. The construction is used in communications (quadrature modulation/demodulation, SSB generation), audio analysis (phase vocoder phase unwrapping), geophysics, and biomedical signal processing. Persistence mechanism: algorithmic computation standard in DSP libraries (scipy.signal.hilbert, MATLAB hilbert) and embedded in communication system designs. [formal: signalis analyticus | substrate: mind | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Instantaneous frequency is a human-made signal processing construct that measures the rate of change of the phase of a signal at each moment in time. It is defined as: f_inst(t) = (1/2π)·dφ(t)/dt, where φ(t) = arg(z(t)) is the instantaneous phase of the analytic signal z(t) = x(t) + j·H{x(t)}, constructed from a real-valued signal x(t) and its Hilbert transform H{x(t)}. Unlike Fourier frequency (which represents a global property of the signal), instantaneous frequency is a local, time-varying quantity that tracks frequency modulation, chirp signals, and time-varying spectral content in real time. Parameters: (1) the phase unwrapping method applied to φ(t) (to avoid discontinuities at ±π), (2) the noise regularization method (to prevent divergence where amplitude is near zero). Persistence mechanism: standard in radar (chirp signal analysis), seismology, speech processing (formant tracking), and biomedical engineering (EEG/ECG frequency modulation analysis), implemented in DSP libraries and embedded in signal analysis instruments. [formal: frequency instantanea | substrate: mind | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Stress is the constructed phonological framework for analyzing prominence asymmetry within words and phrases: certain syllables are marked as stressed (more prominent) relative to their neighbors, and this marking is patterned by linguistic rule. Parameters: (1) degree - relative prominence against neighbors, primary and secondary; (2) realization - the cue bundle carrying stress: increased loudness, increased duration, and, in English, pitch height on the stressed syllable; (3) position - placement within the word, rule-governed in many languages and capable of distinguishing word identity (English 'record' noun vs verb); (4) phrase level - the organization of stresses into rhythmic groups in connected speech. Persistence: stress is realized in every utterance, transcribed in phonology, taught in phonetics and language pedagogy, and codified in dictionaries; it persists as a stable parameter of the linguistic system, changing only slowly across generations. [formal: stressum | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

The Hilbert transform is a linear operator that shifts the phase of every frequency component of a real-valued signal by 90 degrees (π/2 radians). Mathematically, for a signal x(t), the Hilbert transform is: H{x(t)} = (1/π) PV ∫₋∞^∞ x(τ)/(t−τ) dτ, where PV denotes the Cauchy principal value. In the frequency domain, it acts as an all-pass filter with frequency response H(f) = −j·sgn(f), multiplying positive frequencies by −j and negative frequencies by +j. The transform produces the quadrature component of x(t); combining x(t) with its Hilbert transform yields the analytic signal z(t) = x(t) + j·H{x(t)}, from which instantaneous amplitude (envelope), instantaneous phase, and instantaneous frequency can be derived. Parameters: (1) the input signal domain (continuous-time or discrete via DFT-based implementation), (2) handling of the zero-frequency component (typically set to 0). Persistence mechanism: implemented in DSP libraries (scipy.signal.hilbert, MATLAB hilbert), used in communications (SSB modulation/demodulation), geophysics, and vibration analysis. [formal: transform Hilbert | substrate: mind | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Accent is the constructed sociolinguistic concept for the phonological component of a speech variety: the distinctive sound patterns by which a listener identifies a speaker's regional or social origin, in the absence of lexical or grammatical difference. Parameters: (1) phonemic inventory - the distinctive vowel and consonant qualities of the accent; (2) articulation - characteristic manner and place of production; (3) prosodic coloring - the intonational and rhythmic quality that colors the accent; (4) indexing - the geographic and social identity the accent signals to listeners. Accent is the phonological part of dialect: dialect is the whole (phonology + lexicon + grammar), and a speaker can be described by the accent alone while sharing the full dialect. Persistence: accent persists in the speech communities that produce it, is transmitted through first-language acquisition and socialization, and is indexed in dialect atlases and sociolinguistic study; it persists as a stable social marker in individual speakers. [formal: accentus | substrate: language | horizon: generations | explicit: no | epoch: 0.4]

Psycholinguistics is a disciplinary framework for mapping the mental representations and processes underlying language production, comprehension, and acquisition. Parameters: processing models, lexical access, syntactic parsing, memory constraints, experimental paradigms, developmental stages. It persists via peer-reviewed experiments, cognitive models, laboratory protocols, and university curricula that replicate findings across populations.

Corpus-linguistics is a human-made empirical approach to linguistics — the study of language patterns, structures, and usage through systematic analysis of large, representative collections of real-language data (corpora). Two parameters carve the construct: (1) the primary data source is authentic, naturally occurring language recorded in written or spoken form (not introspective or constructed examples), organized into annotated or searchable text collections that sample from defined populations, registers, genres, or time periods; (2) the analytical methods are data-driven and statistical, including frequency analysis, collocation measurement, concordance line examination, n-gram modeling, and distributional semantics, used to discover patterns that may not be predictable from theory alone. Corpus-linguistics persists as a methodological framework that generates empirical descriptions of language (dictionaries, grammars), tests theoretical hypotheses against real usage data, and produces applications in language technology (spell checkers, machine translation, language models), lexicography, and language education. Paradigmatic cases: Brown Corpus frequency analysis, COCA/COHA diachronic corpora, Sketch Engine collocation tools. [formal: corpus-linguistica | substrate: data | horizon: decades | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.02]

The skewness (third standardized moment) of a power spectrum around its spectral centroid. Parameters: (1) a frequency-binned power or magnitude spectrum S[k] for k=0..K-1, (2) the spectral centroid μ = Σ_k f[k]·S[k] / Σ_k S[k], (3) the spectral bandwidth σ = sqrt(Σ_k (f[k]-μ)²·S[k] / Σ_k S[k]). Computation: skewness = Σ_k (f[k]-μ)³·S[k] / (σ³·Σ_k S[k]). Persistence: the scalar value is stored per spectral frame and recomputed when the spectrum changes. Positive skewness indicates a spectrum with a long tail toward higher frequencies; negative skewness indicates a tail toward lower frequencies.

The glottal-source model is a human-made model of the glottal airflow source in speech production, describing the periodic excitation generated by vocal fold vibration. Parameters: fundamental frequency, open quotient, asymmetry coefficient, return phase. Persistence mechanism: the model is formalized as mathematical equations, implemented in speech synthesis software, and taught in speech science; it persists as a reusable component of the source-filter framework. [formal: glottal-source | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.07]

Sociolinguistics is a disciplinary framework for mapping systematic correlations between linguistic variation and social structure. Parameters: speech community, social variables (class, gender, age, ethnicity, region), linguistic variables (phonetic, lexical, syntactic, pragmatic), interactional context and language ideology. It persists via peer-reviewed publications, university curricula, research corpora, and methodological protocols that replicate observations across speech communities.

The root-mean-square energy of a discrete signal over a window of N samples. Parameters: (1) the signal samples x[n] for n in the analysis window, (2) the window length N. Computation: square each sample, compute the arithmetic mean of the squared values, take the square root. Persistence: the scalar value is stored per window and recomputed when samples or window bounds change. This operates directly on time-domain samples, not on any spectral representation.

Accent is the sociolinguistic category that isolates the phonological component of a speech variety as an independently indexable unit: the sound patterns by which a listener identifies a speaker's regional or social origin, abstracted from lexical and grammatical difference. Parameters: (1) isolation rule — the map draws its boundary by holding lexicon and grammar constant and varying only the phonological system (the 'same words, different sound' test); (2) indexed content — the origin the category encodes: regional (e.g., Scots, Geordie, Australian) or social (e.g., RP, AAVE); (3) descriptive levels the map organizes — phonemic inventory, articulation, prosodic coloring; (4) contrast frame — an accent is defined against a reference variety within the same language. Persistence: the category is maintained as an instrument of the discipline — dialect atlases (Survey of English Dialects), sociolinguistic textbooks and curricula, accent-labeling practice in media and pedagogy, and listening-identification tests — drawn, taught, and revised by sociolinguists; it is maintained by the discipline, not transmitted by speakers. [formal: accentus | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A filterbank is a bank of interrelated bandpass filters that decomposes an input signal into multiple frequency sub-bands. Parameters: (1) number of filters — the count of distinct sub-bands; (2) center frequencies — the passband center for each filter; (3) bandwidth — the width of each passband (often constant-Q or constant-percent-bandwidth); (4) overlap factor — whether sub-bands overlap in frequency. The filterbank operates by routing the input signal through each bandpass filter, producing a set of sub-band outputs where each represents the signal energy within a specific frequency range. The persistence mechanism is algorithmic computation: the filterbank is implemented as a cascade or parallel array of filter coefficients in DSP software libraries (librosa, kaldi, MATLAB) and hardware DSP pipelines, applied to signals as a deterministic transformation. [formal: banca filtri | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A cepstrum is the power spectrum of the log-power spectrum of a signal. Computed by: taking the Fourier transform of the signal, computing the log of the magnitude spectrum, then computing the inverse Fourier transform of the log-magnitude spectrum. Parameters: window size for the initial transform, overlap for overlap-add reconstruction. The cepstrum separates periodic structures in the spectrum (such as formant echoes in speech or pitch harmonics) into distinct peaks at quefrency positions corresponding to the delay between reflections. Persistence mechanism: the cepstrum is computed as a deterministic mathematical transform, implemented in speech analysis and audio processing software, and used as an intermediate representation in cepstral feature extraction pipelines. [formal: cepstrum | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A crest-factor is a human-made audio engineering metric that quantifies the ratio of peak amplitude to RMS amplitude of a signal. Parameters: (1) A_peak = max|A(t)| the peak amplitude, (2) A_rms = √(1/T ∫₀ᵀ A(t)² dt) the RMS amplitude over window T. The persistence mechanism is the scalar ratio: CF = A_peak / A_rms. Used to characterize the dynamic profile of audio signals, distinguish percussive from sustained sounds. |crest-factor| CF = A_peak / A_rms |2025-01-01| Ezra

An utterance is the human-constructed concept for a contiguous stretch of speech or writing that participants in a communicative event treat as a single, bounded unit of action. Parameters: (1) physical extent — the actual span of vocal articulation or written symbols, from first sound/symbol to last; (2) communicative boundary — the participants' shared understanding of where this unit begins and ends, which may diverge from grammatical boundaries (an utterance may span multiple sentences or be a fragment of one); (3) functional unit — the utterance performs some recoverable communicative function within the ongoing interaction. Distinction from related constructs: a sentence is a grammatical unit defined by syntactic rules; a speech act is the action performed by an utterance (one utterance may realize multiple speech acts); discourse is the larger organized structure of multiple utterances. Persistence: maintained through transcription conventions, dialogue annotation frameworks, and the analytical practices of pragmatics and discourse analysis. [formal: uterantia | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A bark-spectrogram is a two-dimensional time-frequency matrix where rows are bark-scale frequency bins and columns are temporal frames. Parameters: (1) N bark-scale bins indexed 0..N-1, (2) frame hop size h in samples, (3) window function w applied per frame. Computation: for each frame f, apply FFT to windowed segment, convert linear-frequency indices to bark scale via Bark(f) = 13*arctan(0.00076*f) + 3.5*arctan((f/7500)^2), accumulate energy into bark bins, normalize by bin bandwidth. Persistence: the matrix values are the squared magnitudes accumulated per bark bin, stored as a sequence of N×T matrices. Display: a heatmap with time on the x-axis, Bark units on the y-axis, color representing log-energy.

Lexeme is a human-made conceptual category — the minimal meaningful unit of a language that functions as the basic item in the mental lexicon of speakers. Three parameters carve the construct: (1) minimal meaningfulness: the lexeme carries semantic content that cannot be decomposed into smaller meaningful parts within that language's grammar, distinguishing it from phrases or complex words whose meaning is compositional; (2) identity-independence: the lexeme has a single abstract identity across all its surface forms — inflectional variants (walk/walks/walked/walking) and allomorphic variants (happy/happiness) express the same lexeme, while a shift in core meaning or derivational structure marks a different lexeme; (3) mental reality: lexemes are stored and retrieved by speakers as discrete units in the mental lexicon, not as lists of word forms. Lexemes persist as the atomic referent of grammatical description, lexical semantics, and word-formation rules. [formal: lexema | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Computational linguistics is a disciplinary framework for formalizing linguistic knowledge in algorithms and computational models. Parameters: corpus design, statistical models, symbolic grammars, evaluation metrics, processing pipelines. It persists via open-source software, benchmark datasets, peer-reviewed publications, and university curricula that replicate model performance across tasks.

Linguistic register is the map of the system of situationally differentiated language varieties a speech community develops and maintains — the varieties a community deploys for different communicative situations (colloquial, formal, technical, ceremonial, professional) — carved along three parameters. (1) The situational axis: the dimensions along which the varieties are organized are field (the subject matter and activity in which the language is deployed), tenor (the social relations and roles between participants), and mode (the channel and the participatory structure of the discourse); a variety is a conventionalized set of lexical, grammatical, and prosodic choices indexed to the situation, so that the same speaker deploys different varieties in different situations. (2) The boundary lines that separate the map from its neighbours: register is indexed to situation, which distinguishes it from dialect (indexed to region and social group) and from genre (a type of discourse text rather than a variety of the language itself); and it is distinct from the institutional register — an official list maintained by an authority with legal or institutional force — in that a linguistic register is updated by the speech community's convention, not by institutional mandate, and no authority stands behind its entries. (3) The map, not the territory: the entry names the systematic description the community and the discipline build over the natural variation of speech — the inventory of varieties and the dimensions that organize it — not the natural variation itself. Persistence: the varieties persist as social convention — acquired in socialization, maintained through institutional reinforcement (courts, academies, professions, liturgy), and relearned by each generation; the map persists as the stable sub-field of linguistics called register analysis, its dimensions codified in textbooks and corpora. [formal: regiter linguae | substrate: behavior | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.05]

Neurolinguistics is a human-made interdisciplinary field — the study of the neural and biological mechanisms that underlie language acquisition, processing, representation, and comprehension. Two parameters carve the construct: (1) the explanatory level is biological/neural (brain anatomy, neural circuits, electrophysiological responses, neuroimaging data, lesion studies, and molecular markers), not purely behavioral or computational; (2) the phenomenon explained is language in its full range — phonology, syntax, semantics, pragmatics, lexicon, acquisition, and breakdown — treated as operations implemented by neural systems. Neurolinguistics persists as an active research enterprise that generates testable hypotheses about how the brain implements language, uses these hypotheses to interpret clinical conditions (aphasia, dyslexia, speech disorders), and informs brain-computer interfaces for language restoration. Paradigmatic methods: fMRI and EEG mapping of language tasks, lesion-symptom mapping in aphasia patients, intracranial electrophysiology, and computational modeling of neural language processing. [formal: neurolinguistica | substrate: brain | horizon: decades | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.02]

Intonation is the constructed linguistic framework for analyzing pitch-contour organization in spoken language: the way fundamental frequency rises and falls across the duration of an utterance, and the way those movements are patterned by linguistic rule rather than speaker whim. Parameters: (1) pitch contour - the F0 trajectory across the utterance, rising, falling, or level; (2) tone unit - the stretch of speech over which a single contour operates, delimited by pauses; (3) nuclear stress - the syllable carrying the principal tone of the tone unit; (4) grammatical and attitudinal function - contour used to mark clause type (interrogative vs declarative), focus, and attitude (e.g., English rising terminals for yes-no questions). Persistence: intonation is realized in every produced utterance, analyzed in intonation notation (e.g., ToBI), taught in language pedagogy, and studied in phonology; it persists as long as speech carries meaning through pitch. [formal: intonatio | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Historical linguistics is a disciplinary framework for reconstructing diachronic change in language systems from attested corpora. Parameters: comparative method, sound change laws, attestation dates, textual corpora, reconstruction techniques. It persists via published reconstructions, philological editions, comparative datasets, and university curricula that transmit methodological standards across generations.

The source-filter model is a human-made mathematical model of speech production that decomposes the speech signal generation into a source component, typically the glottal airflow with fundamental frequency, and a filter component, the vocal tract transfer function shaping formants. Parameters: source excitation model, filter order, formant frequencies and bandwidths, glottal pulse shape. Persistence mechanism: the model is formalized in equations, implemented in speech synthesis and analysis software, and taught in speech science curricula; it persists as a reusable theoretical framework. [formal: source-filter-model | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.07]

A sociolect is a variety of language associated with a particular social group or social class, distinguished by systematic conventions in lexicon, pronunciation, and grammar that mark group membership. It operates through shared linguistic practices that emerge from common social experiences, institutional affiliations, or cultural positions — distinct from dialects (which are geographic) and registers (which are situational). Parameters include the social boundary that defines the group (occupation, education level, socioeconomic status, subculture), the degree of linguistic convergence or divergence from the broader vernacular, and the social indexicality of distinctive forms. Persistence mechanism: sociolects persist as living practice within groups — reproduced through social interaction, reinforced through identity marking, and maintained through the group's internal need for linguistic solidarity, independent of any formal codification or institutional support. [formal: sociolectus | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.50]

Cognitive-linguistics is a human-made approach to linguistics — the study of language as a manifestation of general cognitive abilities, including categorization, conceptualization, metaphorical reasoning, and embodied experience. Two parameters carve the construct: (1) the explanatory framework denies that language operates as an autonomous module separate from general cognition; language structure reflects domain-general cognitive mechanisms like attention, memory, pattern recognition, and conceptual blending; (2) the empirical evidence comes from cross-linguistic analysis of how semantic structure, syntactic patterns, and figurative language systematically reflect cognitive universals (spatial reasoning, embodiment, force-dynamics) rather than language-internal formal rules. Cognitive-linguistics persists as a theoretical framework that produces models of construction grammar, conceptual metaphor theory, and cognitive semantics, generating testable predictions about language use, acquisition, and processing that compete with modularist accounts. Paradigmatic cases: conceptual metaphor analysis (e.g., ARGUMENT IS WAR), construction grammar descriptions, image-schema theory. [formal: cognitio-linguistica | substrate: mind | horizon: decades | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

An instantaneous-amplitude is a human-made signal processing construct that extracts the time-varying envelope of an analytic signal as its complex magnitude. Parameters: (1) z(t) = x(t) + j·H{x(t)} the analytic signal, (2) φ(t) = arg(z(t)) the instantaneous phase. The persistence mechanism is pointwise magnitude: A(t) = |z(t)| = √(x(t)² + H{x(t)}²). Used for amplitude demodulation and envelope analysis in communication systems. |instantaneous-amplitude| A(t) = |z(t)| = √(x(t)² + H{x(t)}²) |2025-01-01| Ezra

Derivation is a human-made morphological operation — the process by which a language creates a new lexeme from an existing one by adding derivational material. Three parameters carve the construct: (1) lexeme change: the output is a new lexeme with a distinct dictionary identity from the input (happy → happiness is one lexeme becoming another; walk → walked is NOT derivation, because walked is an inflected form of the same lexeme as walk). This lexeme-change criterion is the decisive boundary from inflection. (2) derivational material: the operation is carried by a bound morpheme (affix) or, in some languages, by a change of stress, vowel, or other internal modification that contributes derivational meaning (English sing → song: an ablaut-derived noun; by contrast the tense forms sang and sung remain inflected forms of the same lexeme as sing). (3) conventionalized meaning: the derivational material contributes a systematic, predictable meaning (-ness 'state of being', un- 'negation', -er 'agent') that transforms the input lexeme's meaning in a rule-governed way. Paradigmatic cases: happy + -ness → happiness (new lexeme); write → writer (new lexeme, agentive). Derivation persists as a productive rule — speakers coin new derived lexemes on the fly — and as a stable category of grammatical description: derivational affixes are catalogued in the morphological inventory of each language. [formal: derivatio | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]
